label: Claude Opus 5.5
output:
**Two short on a Thursday**

Bridget has asked me to write this month's piece, and I should say at the outset that she has an ulterior motive. We need two more people for the Thursday tea trolley in the day unit. I'll come to the practical details, but first I want to clear up a misunderstanding, because I shared it myself until four years ago.

I used to assume that volunteering at a hospice must be one of two things: either harrowing, or a job for people with nursing training and endless reserves of patience. I had no training, and anyone who worked with me will tell you I wasn't overburdened with patience either. I spent 41 years as a bookkeeper, most of them for a builders' merchant in Dereham, and when I retired I found that I had no regular reason to go out most weeks. For about eighteen months I drifted. I went out less and less, and I noticed it. In March 2022 I started on the Thursday trolley, and Thursdays fixed that. I'd like to tell you it was a noble calling, but the truth is I needed somewhere to be.

So here is what it actually involves. The day therapy unit sees somewhere between 14 and 18 patients on a Thursday afternoon. Some come for the art group, some for the hand massage, and a good many come for the company. Most of them go home afterwards. We take the trolley round from half past one until four, and we make tea, pour squash, hand out biscuits and chat.

You don't need any nursing skill whatsoever. You need to be able to push a trolley, remember who takes what, and listen. The remembering turns out to be where four decades of keeping ledgers straight comes in handy. Mr Hollis, a retired signalman, takes two sugars and tells me about the 1953 floods every week, slightly differently each time. I've stopped correcting the dates. It's his story, and it improves with the telling.

Nor do you need to be graceful. In my very first week I tipped an entire jug of milk over the trolley. A patient called Pat laughed so much she had to be given a tissue, and she told me afterwards it was the best afternoon she'd had in a month. I've not repeated the performance, but I mention it so you know the bar is not high.

It isn't a sad place on a Thursday, mostly. It's noisy and rather jolly, and there's a good deal of arguing about the bourbon biscuits, which always go first. We now hide a packet for the late group. I won't pretend every week is like that. Some days are hard, and you feel them. When that happens the staff look after us properly, and you are not left on your own with it. But those afternoons are not most afternoons.

Now the practical part. There are four of us on a rota meant for six. We lost two over the summer, one to Sheffield to be nearer her grandchildren and one to a knee operation, and neither for any reason to do with the work. The commitment is one Thursday a fortnight, 1.30 to 4pm. Bridget does the induction herself, which takes about two hours, and there's a short food hygiene course online that the hospice pays for. That's it. Nobody will ask you to do more than you've agreed to.

If you're even slightly tempted, come to the volunteer open afternoon on **Tuesday 24 November at 2pm in the Willow Room**. There will be tea and biscuits, you can ask whatever you like, and there's no obligation at all. If an afternoon doesn't suit, ring Bridget on the volunteering line and she'll happily talk it through.

And if it isn't for you, perhaps you know someone it would suit. Someone recently retired, perhaps, who has gone a bit quiet. Bring them along on the 24th. I would very much like to see at least two new faces in the Willow Room, and I'm told I'm quite good at remembering how people take their tea.

I'll save you a bourbon.
